games.explanation: Wheeler is the better pitcher, nobody's arguing that, but the price on the Cardinals treats this like a mismatch when the two clubs are effectively even by every rating that matters. St. Louis has actually solved this exact profile better than the market thinks, and Iván Herrera in particular is the kind of right-handed bat who punishes velocity, sitting on a .371 xwOBA that plays anywhere. Leahy is not going to overpower Schwarber and Harper, but he doesn't have to be great in a park where the projected margin is a single run. At +147, you're getting a coin flip priced like a blowout, which is the entire reason to click it.

Dustin May's line score has been flattering him all year, and the underlying contact quality tells the real story about a righty who walks nearly as many hitters as he strikes out. San Diego runs a top of the order built to punish exactly that profile, with Tatis and Machado sitting on the kind of hard contact that turns May's 44.8 hard-hit rate into actual damage. Ray isn't the sharper name on the marquee but he's been the sharper pitcher, and the gap between his xwOBA-against and May's is where this whole ticket lives. Getting the better team at plus money in a game the market has priced as a coin flip is the entire pitch, and +105 is the receipt.

Bryce Miller's stat line reads like a pitcher the market keeps giving the benefit of the doubt to, and tonight the Yankees are the wrong lineup to keep extending that credit. Righties are slugging him at a .355 xwOBA clip, which is exactly the profile Ben Rice has been feasting on all year, and Grisham behind him keeps the damage rolling from the same side. Warren isn't a shutdown arm, but he doesn't need to be against a Seattle order that thins out fast after Arozarena. At -124, you're getting the better team, the better lineup matchup, and a starter the board is still overrating.

Our sim lands on a four-to-five kind of game, exactly the sort of margin where the extra run and a half is the whole ballgame.
